posts.body:
Most AI crawlers do not run JavaScript. GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot: they fetch your HTML and parse it. No hydration, no effects, no client-side fetches. If your site is a React SPA, here is what ChatGPT's crawler actually receives:
That's it. That's the page.

A thing that confuses people:

You can rank fine in Google and be completely absent from ChatGPT.

Google renders JavaScript. It has for years.
The AI crawlers mostly do not.

Same site, two very different views. Your SEO tool only ever showed you the first one.

If you blocked AI crawlers in robots.txt, check which ones.

GPTBot = training. Blocking it costs you nothing in visibility.
OAI-SearchBot = the index behind ChatGPT search.
ChatGPT-User = fetches your page when someone pastes your link.

Blocking the last two removes you from answers people actually read. A lot of "block AI" guides conflate all three.

Every agency is getting the same client question right now: "why don't we show up in ChatGPT?"

Before you buy a $300/month monitoring tool to answer it, check something cheaper.

Most AI crawlers don't execute JavaScript. They fetch raw HTML and parse what is there. If the client's site renders client-side — a React SPA, a Next.js app with everything behind "use client", a Squarespace page built out of summary blocks — the crawler receives an empty container.

No amount of prompt monitoring fixes that. It just tells you, monthly, that you are still absent.

The diagnostic takes one command:

curl -s -A "GPTBot" https://clientsite.com | grep -c "some sentence from the page"

If that returns 0, you have found the problem, and it is not a content problem.

posts.title: PSA: your SPA is invisible to AI crawlers, and your Google ranking won't tell you
posts.body:
Spent a while digging into this and it surprised me enough to write up.

Googlebot renders JavaScript — it has a full rendering pipeline. So a client-side React app can index fine and rank fine.

The AI crawlers are a different pipeline entirely. GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot — these fetch the HTML and parse it. No JS execution.

So the test everyone runs ("we rank on Google, we're fine") is measuring the wrong crawler.

Quick way to check your own site:

    curl -s -A "GPTBot" https://yoursite.com | sed 's/<[^>]*>//g' | tr -s ' \n' ' ' | wc -w

If that number is under ~100 and your page clearly has more content than that, the content is arriving via JavaScript and the crawler isn't getting it.

Fixes depend on stack — SSR, static generation, or a prerender step. Next.js App Router is fine by default unless you've pushed pages behind "use client". Astro and Gatsby are fine. Plain Vite/CRA SPAs are the bad case.

Also worth checking: whether your robots.txt is blocking the *retrieval* crawlers vs the *training* crawlers. Those are different bots with different consequences and a lot of "block AI scrapers" snippets going around block both.

Ran the AI-readability audit across 50 sites I could find in one niche.

Median score: 61/100.
Worst offender: a $200/mo SaaS whose entire marketing site returns 0 readable words to a non-rendering crawler.

The pattern is nearly always the same: a beautiful client-rendered site that no answer engine can read.
